# Ticket-to-Machine — Supporting Technical Detail (Standalone Edition) {.unnumbered}

The Closure Necessity argument holds that native cloud and virtualization consoles are excellent at changing state and structurally incapable of producing the evidence an assessor can trace: a console shows current state, while an evidence record has to show who owns a finding, the clock they are working against, the approval trail for any exception, and a re-test that proves closure. Azure Policy, AWS Config, and vSphere Configuration Profiles all genuinely remediate; none of them, alone, answers those four questions. That gap is closed by a coordination layer — ServiceNow — sitting in front of the native tools rather than replacing them, running a five-step loop: **test → detect drift → raise a typed task against the reconciled CI → actuate on the native surface → close with evidence.**

The four sections below carry the supporting detail behind that argument. §1 shows the same loop running over a second control family, identity lifecycle, in a deployable implementation rather than in prose. §2 extends the argument into access governance. §3 sets out the one domain that deliberately does not take this path. §4 surveys the vendor landscape and the build-vs-buy question a critical reviewer will raise.

## 1. The Same Loop in a Second Control Domain: Identity Lifecycle

The Closure Necessity claim is usually argued over configuration, vulnerability, and patch controls — CM-6, RA-5, SI-2 — because that is where the drift is most visible. The claim does not stop at that boundary. The same five-step discipline runs over a different control family entirely: **AC-2/AC-3/AC-6 identity lifecycle**, where the "drift" is an account that should not exist, an entitlement nobody re-certified, or a privilege that outlived its purpose.

That is not only an argument. A deployable ServiceNow scoped application implements it, and ships as buildable source rather than as a design document: script includes carrying the orchestration and the platform clients, automated test specifications that exercise the refusals, control maps binding catalog items to real actuator methods, and build-time gates that fail the build when those bindings are missing.

**The orchestration contract.** Every governed identity request runs through five ordered clauses — Origin, Authorize, Elevate, Actuate, Evidence, the MACD-R lifecycle (move/add/change/delete, plus recertify). The chain is ordered and fail-closed: a clause that cannot satisfy itself stops the request rather than passing it on, and a request that stops is never recorded as closed. That property is the whole point. A coordination layer that raises a task and then trusts the caller to have done the right thing reproduces the ticket-to-human failure mode with extra steps.

| Coordination step | MACD-R clause | What the implementation enforces |
|---|---|---|
| Raise against the reconciled record | 1 · Origin | Resolves the originating request record — the catalog request or upstream governance request that authorizes this change — and refuses when it cannot. A caller with no lineage record cannot invoke the chain at all, so there is no path by which an identity change exists without a request behind it. A dedicated negative test exercises that refusal directly. |
| Authorize the change | 2 · Authorize | A pre-flight gate checks separation of duties (the requester and the approver cannot be the same person) and least-privilege expiry (an entitlement past its review date does not silently persist), fail-closed — the absence of a positive answer is a refusal, not a pass. |
| Actuate on the native surface | 3 · Elevate, 4 · Actuate | A time-boxed privileged activation is granted first, and its identifier is required downstream: no activation identifier, no actuation. Standing privilege is therefore never the mechanism by which a change succeeds. The write itself then runs against the native surface — Graph/ARM for cloud objects, or Active Directory through a domain-joined, in-boundary MID Server. |
| Close with evidence | 4 · Verify, 5 · Evidence | Post-state is re-read before any closure record is written: a 2xx response from the write is not closure. Exactly one evidence record is written per request, and that holds for a *refused* task as much as a successful one — a refusal is itself an evidenced outcome, not a silent no-op. |

**Who actuates, and under what identity.** Directory writes — creating a user, disabling an account, resetting a password, adding a group member — are dispatched through the in-boundary MID Server under a delegated, least-privilege service account, explicitly never a Domain Admin and never an operator's interactive session. The coordination layer itself writes only its own workflow records; it raises, routes, and evidences, and does not write to the estate. That distinction matters more than it first reads: the platform clients in the same application *do* actuate the tenant, but always under a delegated service identity scoped to the operations they perform, never as the coordination layer wielding standing tenant access.

**The two legs are not symmetric, and the design says so.** The cloud leg re-reads post-state through the platform API before closing, so verification and actuation sit in the same synchronous path. The directory leg dispatches asynchronously through the MID Server and returns a dispatch receipt — an acknowledgement that the instruction was queued, not a claim about the resulting directory state — with separate read-back operations available to establish that state. Both legs end at the same guarantee, but the directory leg reaches it in two steps rather than one, and conflating the receipt with the outcome is exactly the mistake the design is arranged to prevent.

This is the same discipline the coordination layer applies to configuration drift — ingest the native state read-only, reconcile every finding to the authoritative CMDB CI before a task is raised, and re-read the native surface after actuation to stamp the re-test evidence on the task. Actuation stays on the native surface; the coordination layer never writes the resource; and "closed" means a re-read confirmed the change, not that a script returned success.

**Proving the discipline rather than asserting it.** The negative test specifications are automated tests that the chain actually refuses what it claims to refuse: self-approval, standing privilege, an unreconciled target, a missing origin record, and hostile input parameters. Each is a refusal that would be invisible in a passing happy-path suite, which is why they are written as negative cases. The build-time gates are gates, not documentation: a build fails where a catalog item claims autonomous write with no governance decision behind it, or where a control-map entry names an actuator method that does not exist. Together they close the gap between what an architecture document says and what a deployed instance will actually do.

**Two operational details worth naming**, because they are where doctrine meets habit. The admin-initiated password reset is the approver-gated fallback *behind* self-service reset, not the primary path — the common case never reaches an approver, and the uncommon one always does. And the daily sync-health check, which in the as-found estate meant an operator using RDP to the sync host to eyeball it, is a read-only automated reconciliation job: the same information, obtained without a human holding interactive credentials on a directory-adjacent server. Neither is dramatic. Both are the kind of thing that quietly decides whether the ticket-to-machine principle survives contact with the operations floor.

::: {.callout-caution}
## Honest scope note
This is reference material, not a turnkey product, and it says so in its own framing: the script includes, test specifications, control maps, and build-time gates ship as source, but the ServiceNow platform records themselves — tables, ACLs, the assembled update set — are built on an instance and exported, not shipped pre-built. It carries a no-warranty disclaimer. Treat it as a working reference implementation to build from and test against, not as evidence that any particular agency instance is already running it.

Two narrower limits are worth naming rather than glossing. The delegation claim — that the service account is least-privilege and never a Domain Admin — is asserted in the implementation's own documentation and has not been independently verified; an effective-permissions dump against that account would settle it and remains an open item. And the build-time gates verify that actuators and governance decisions exist, which is a real guarantee but not the same one as "the code does what this section says it does." That broader claim has no equivalent automated check.
:::

**What this adds to the argument.** Showing the pattern is identical across four vendor stacks establishes that it is not a per-vendor accident. Showing it identical across control *domains* — configuration drift and identity lifecycle — establishes something stronger: that the loop is a property of what evidence requires, not of what any one product happens to expose. Read against §2's extension into access governance, identity lifecycle is where that domain's coordination loop is not only argued but implemented and testable end to end.

## 2. Access Governance and SailPoint ISC Governance

The argument so far concerns configuration, vulnerability, and patch controls — the domain the ServiceNow-fronting pattern is built and deployed for today. It extends cleanly to a second domain: **access governance** — who has an identity, who granted it, and who periodically recertifies it — resting on a different set of controls, principally AC-2 (Account Management), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), and AC-6 (Least Privilege).

Azure RBAC role assignments and AWS IAM policies can be inspected and even remediated natively, but a native IAM console has the identical evidence gap the configuration-drift argument describes: a role binding is not, by itself, a record of who requested it, who approved it, and when it was last reviewed. **SailPoint ISC Governance (the CIEM add-on)** performs exactly the detection function this domain needs — over-privileged accounts, entitlements idle 90+ days, over-broad role bindings — natively across Azure, AWS, and GCP.

::: {.callout-tip}
## One front door, not two
AC-2/AC-3/AC-6 close for Azure RBAC and AWS IAM entitlements using the identical test → detect drift → raise task → actuate-native → close-with-evidence loop as configuration drift. This deliberately does **not** stand up a second, SailPoint-fronted coordination layer. SailPoint ISC Governance is one more detection engine feeding the same ServiceNow pipeline every other control family uses — structurally identical to how Security Hub, Defender for Cloud, and Aria Operations feed it. That choice is consistent with SailPoint's own architecture, which routes findings into ServiceNow rather than around it (§4).
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## SAM and ISC are two SailPoint products, not one name for one thing
Everything above concerns **SailPoint ISC Governance**. Where an agency also runs an access-request and certification portal under a local brand — **SAM (Systems Access Management)** is one such brand for a **SailPoint IdentityIQ** deployment — that is a different product, not the same one renamed, and the difference is operational rather than cosmetic.

| | **IdentityIQ**, e.g. branded SAM | **Identity Security Cloud** + CIEM |
|---|---|---|
| Hosting | Customer-hosted, on agency infrastructure | SailPoint-hosted SaaS |
| Integration surface | SCIM 2.0 plus a core REST API tied to the installed release | Continuously-versioned cloud REST API |
| Direction into ServiceNow | Pushes an approved access request in, correlated to a RITM, with closure written back | Pushes cloud-entitlement findings in, as one more detection engine |
| Authorization posture | Inside the agency's own boundary — no additional cloud authorization to buy | SailPoint-hosted, so it carries the authorization question every SaaS dependency carries |

An integration built against one product's API surface does not transfer to the other, and the two are scoped, licensed, and versioned separately. Neither fact weakens the one-front-door conclusion above — both converge on ServiceNow — but a plan that treats them as a single SailPoint integration will under-scope the work.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## Honest limit that remains — VMware/vCenter identity governance
No evidence was found, after direct research, that SailPoint's CIEM add-on reaches VMware/vCenter permissions — every source describes AWS/Azure/GCP coverage only. This is a genuinely open gap, not a scope deferred by choice, and it should be stated plainly rather than papered over with an implication of coverage that does not exist.
:::

## 3. The Certificates Exception — Why PKI Doesn't Take the Same Path

Certificates are a large share of the actual operational work in this estate, which makes it tempting to assume they belong on the same ServiceNow-fronted path as everything else. They don't — not for the routine lifecycle — and the reason is a deliberate doctrine call, not an oversight.

**The reasoning is volume, not principle.** A CM-6 configuration-drift finding happens occasionally and each one is worth a human decision. A certificate estate with 30–90 day validity periods generates **thousands of issuance and renewal events a week**. Routing each through a ServiceNow approval ticket would not add rigor; it would make the queue meaningless and train reviewers to rubber-stamp it. There is no staffing level at which manual key custody closes SC-12 for a machine-scale estate: the arithmetic, not the ambition, is the constraint.

So IA-5(2), SC-12, and SC-17 close with **protocol-enforced automation** instead — ACME/SCEP/EST issuance gates, CAA records making issuance policy machine-enforced at the DNS layer, and short-lived certificates with non-renewal replacing revocation as the normal end-of-life path. This is the same underlying principle as the rest of the argument — evidence has to come from something stronger than "trust me, it's fine" — applied correctly to a domain where the volume math rules out ticket-per-event. No owner is named for routine issuance, because none needs to be.

**What still needs the front door.** The exceptions and anomalies in the certificate estate are structurally identical to a CM-6 finding and belong on the same ServiceNow path as everything else: onboarding a new CA, approving a non-standard certificate lifetime, a trust-anchor change, or — the important one — a **drift finding from the certificate inventory**, such as an unknown-issuer certificate discovered or a CAA-violation attempt. Those are rare, high-stakes, human-decision events. Routine issuance within policy is not one of them.

**Recommended tool: CyberArk Certificate Manager (Venafi).** Where the agency already runs CyberArk for privileged access management, CyberArk Certificate Manager is the same vendor relationship extended to certificates rather than a new one — CyberArk acquired Venafi in 2024. It is FedRAMP authorized, discovers and orchestrates certificates across CAs without needing to be the issuing CA itself, and integrates with ServiceNow for the CMDB and exception side.

The competing option, **Keyfactor for Government CLAaaS**, achieved FedRAMP Moderate authorization in May 2026 and has a deeper native ServiceNow ITOM/ACME integration plus its own issuing CA (EJBCA) — a stronger single-vendor pick where there is no existing relationship, though consolidating onto the vendor already in the estate generally outweighs that for an agency with a CyberArk contract, support relationship, and operational familiarity already in place.

Neither vendor's VMware/vCenter certificate coverage could be confirmed externally. Treat that as an open question — consistent with the VMware blind spot found across every tool surveyed here — not an assumption of coverage.

## 4. Vendor Landscape and Build-vs-Buy (2026-07-28)

The central claim — that a native console cannot be the evidence system of record — is not a position held in isolation. Independent research, done the same week the argument was drafted, backs it directly and sharpens several points:

- **The market agrees on the structural claim.** *"CSPM complements GRC — findings need owners and closure proof"* and *"no single tool covers everything inside a FedRAMP boundary… programs rely on a coordinated stack"* (Continuum GRC; Knox Systems, 2026) — independent confirmation of the Key Finding, not a restatement of it.
- **ServiceNow↔VMware integration is not greenfield.** Real vendor-built connectors exist today: the **VMware Aria Operations Management Pack for ServiceNow** and the **VCF Automation ITSM plugin**, offering CMDB mapping and Day-2 catalog operations out of the box. The ServiceNow–VMware surface should be understood as built, not unbuilt.
- **A commercial FedRAMP 20x KSI product already exists.** **C1Secure SmartRAMP 20x** (launched July 2026) runs natively on the ServiceNow platform, validates KSI evidence on FedRAMP's own cadence, and auto-opens Integrated Risk Management remediation — a real alternative to a custom-built scoped application for the KSI-attestation slice specifically. Worth a build-vs-buy pass before further custom investment there.
- **SailPoint's own architecture confirms §2's framing**, not a SailPoint-as-second-front-door version of it. SailPoint ISC and its CIEM add-on natively govern AWS/Azure/GCP cloud IAM entitlements — over-privileged accounts, idle entitlements, over-broad roles — and that capability is genuinely strong. But SailPoint's own integration documentation routes findings *into* ServiceNow's Service Desk for ticketing and audit tracking. Even SailPoint does not claim to be a standalone evidence and ticketing system. No evidence was found of SailPoint CIEM reaching VMware/vCenter permissions specifically; that gap is confirmed, not assumed.
- **Alternative architectures a critical reviewer will raise.** **Wiz** is the only major CNAPP with explicit native VMware vSphere support alongside AWS/Azure/GCP/OCI — a candidate to replace three separate native per-CSP posture engines with one, without changing the ServiceNow-front-door architecture. **Vanta / RegScale / Paramify** represent a different bet entirely: an OSCAL-first, FedRAMP-20x-native compliance platform that self-generates the KSI package, bypassing ServiceNow/SailPoint coordination altogether (Vanta is FedRAMP 20x Moderate Authorized as of April 2026). Neither is adopted by the recommendation here, but both are the alternatives a sharp reviewer will name — cited so the argument isn't caught flat-footed by the question.

**The consistency implication.** Because SailPoint's own architecture already routes through ServiceNow rather than around it, the identity and access-governance domain (§2) should extend the *same* ServiceNow-fronted loop that configuration, vulnerability, and patch controls use — SailPoint CIEM as one more detection engine feeding ServiceNow, structurally identical to how Security Hub, Defender for Cloud, and Aria Operations feed it — rather than standing up SailPoint as a second, parallel coordination layer. One front door, not two.

## 5. Vendor Currency

::: {.callout-important}
## Vendor currency caveat — read before building a Project Plan on this document
This document names specific, dated vendor capabilities — SmartRAMP 20x, the VMware Aria/ServiceNow connectors, SailPoint CIEM's cloud coverage, Wiz, Vanta, CyberArk/Keyfactor — and this market moves in weeks, not review cycles. Every vendor claim here, including §2's SailPoint coverage and §3's CyberArk/Keyfactor comparison, is a dated snapshot rather than a standing commitment. **Confirming current roadmaps directly with ServiceNow, SailPoint, VMware/Broadcom, and each CSP (Microsoft, AWS, GCP) is essential before any claim here becomes the basis of an implementation Project Plan, procurement action, or acquisition decision.**
:::

## 6. Authority Mapping and Non-Compliance Exposure

The argument throughout reasons from control families. This section states the specific guidelines behind those claims in one place, and what an agency is actually exposed to when the remediation obligation goes unclosed.

### 6.1 NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 — the controls this loop closes

The catalog is **NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5**, at the **FedRAMP Moderate** baseline.

| Control | Title | What closes it in this loop | FedRAMP 20x KSI |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CM-6** | Configuration Settings | Native engine detects baseline drift; the coordination layer supplies owner, clock, approval, re-test evidence | KSI-CMT |
| **RA-5** | Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning | Native scanner detects; the SLA clock and the owned task live in ServiceNow | KSI-MLA |
| **SI-2** | Flaw Remediation | Native patch/remediation actuates; closure evidence is the ticket record | KSI-SVC, KSI-MLA |
| **AC-2** | Account Management | Entitlement detection feeds a governed request-and-approval record | KSI-IAM |
| **AC-3** | Access Enforcement | Role binding actuated natively, authorized by an approved record | KSI-IAM |
| **AC-6** | Least Privilege | Over-privilege findings become owned, clocked remediation tasks | KSI-IAM |
| **CA-2** | Control Assessments | Scheduled control test reads actioned posture, renders pass/fail/partial with evidence | KSI-MLA |
| **CA-5** | Plan of Action and Milestones | Any fail becomes an owned POA&M item with milestone and closure evidence | KSI-MLA |
| **CA-7** | Continuous Monitoring | Roll-up emitted as OSCAL assessment-results and KSI evidence | KSI-MLA |
| **IA-5(2)** | Public Key-Based Authentication | Protocol-enforced issuance, not ticket-per-event — the deliberate exception | KSI-IAM |
| **SC-17** | PKI Certificates | Same exception path; anomalies route through the front door, routine issuance does not | KSI-IAM |

: Controls this loop closes, and the KSI each feeds {.striped .hover}

Every row above is marked *not tool-attestable on its own* in the underlying control-closure analysis. The native engine is necessary and not sufficient; the ownership, clock, approval, and evidence record is what makes the control assessable. The Rev 5 Moderate baseline enhancements that actually mandate automation for this argument are **CM-3(2), CM-5(1), CM-6(1), and SI-2(2)**, each checked against FedRAMP's published baseline profile rather than asserted.

### 6.2 FedRAMP 20x — what the loop emits, and on what clock

- **Evidence emission (CA-7).** The closed task stream is lifted into assessed control state and emitted as OSCAL assessment-results plus KSI evidence into the authorization package.
- **KSI families touched:** KSI-CMT (change management), KSI-MLA (monitoring, logging, auditing), KSI-IAM (identity and access management), KSI-SVC (service configuration).
- **KSI-CMT-RMV / VTD / RVP** — redeploy version-controlled resources rather than modify directly. RMV is qualified *wherever reasonable*: an engineering preference with a documented-exception path, not a prohibition.
- **The SLA clock is a published table, not a policy sentiment.** FedRAMP's Vulnerability Detection and Response ruleset (**VDR-TFR-PVR**) sets remediation timeframes by PAIN rating crossed with exploitability and internet-reachability — 4 to 192 days — plus KEV-catalog-driven due dates regardless of PAIN rating. A console has no mechanism to enforce that clock against an owner.

**What 20x obligates is cadence and format, not merely a one-time package.** KSI evidence is a continuous obligation; evidence that was true at authorization and is never refreshed is itself a continuous-monitoring deficiency, independent of whether the underlying control still holds.

### 6.3 CISA BOD 25-01 — the remediation row *is* this loop

::: {.callout-note}
## Attribution — BOD 25-01 is CISA's, not OPM's
Binding Operational Directives are issued by **CISA**, under its directive authority over federal civilian executive branch agencies. OPM issues memoranda and HR-domain guidance; it does not issue BODs. The directive governing the M365/SCuBA scope this document touches is CISA [BOD 25-01](https://cyber.dhs.gov/bod/25-01/), *Implementing Secure Practices for Cloud Services*.
:::

| # | BOD 25-01 obligation | Nature of the work | Addressed by this loop? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Report every in-scope M365 tenant and its system-owning component | Administrative, one-time | No — inventory action |
| 2 | Configure each tenant to the published SCuBA Secure Configuration Baselines | Architectural, ongoing as baselines revise | Partly — the loop closes drift against the baseline |
| 3 | Deploy ScubaGear against every in-scope tenant | Mechanical | No — tool install |
| 4 | Integrate ScubaGear output with CISA's continuous-monitoring infrastructure | Mechanical, then ongoing | No — feed wiring |
| 5 | **Remediate deviations from the baselines** | **Architectural, open-ended** | **Yes — this is precisely the loop** |

: BOD 25-01's five obligations, and which one this loop is for {.striped .hover}

Four of the five rows are satisfiable without closing a single finding: report a tenant name, install a PowerShell tool, wire up a feed. **Row 5 is the architectural one, and it is the row the directive is actually for.** An assessment report that faithfully lists forty deviations every week satisfies rows 1–4 and fails row 5.

**Forward-looking — BOD 26-04.** CISA [BOD 26-04](https://cyber.dhs.gov/bod/26-04/) (*Prioritizing Security*) replaces flat remediation clocks with a risk-based SLA and carries a mandatory adoption deadline of **2026-12-07**. Any remediation-SLA design started now should be checked against it rather than against the older flat clock.

### 6.4 What non-compliance actually costs an agency

| Authority | What makes it binding | Who acts on a failure | What actually happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| CISA BOD 25-01 | Binding operational directive authority over federal civilian executive branch agencies | CISA, reporting to OMB and the agency head | Status is tracked and reported; unclosed deviations persist as a reported deficiency and accumulate visibly |
| NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | Not self-executing — it binds through FISMA and OMB Circular A-130, which require an authorization built on the catalog | Agency Inspector General; OMB | Control deficiencies become audit findings and POA&M items; sustained failures can be escalated to a material weakness |
| FedRAMP 20x continuous monitoring | Authorization is conditional on maintained, current evidence | Authorizing Official; FedRAMP PMO | Stale or absent KSI evidence puts authorized status at risk — corrective action, and in the limit suspension or withdrawal |
| The ATO itself | A revocable risk acceptance, not a permanent grant | The agency's Authorizing Official | An AO can shorten the authorization term, attach conditions, or decline to reauthorize on the strength of an open findings list |

: Non-compliance exposure by authority {.striped .hover}

**The honest shape of the exposure.** None of these authorities carries a fine, and it is worth saying so plainly rather than implying a penalty that does not exist. The consequences are of three kinds: an **authorization** that can be conditioned, shortened, or withdrawn; **audit findings** that persist across reporting cycles and compound; and a **deviation list that grows**, which is itself the documentary evidence that the remediation obligation went unmet. The third is the one that matters most in practice — an assessment tool running faithfully against an unremediated estate produces an accurate, lengthening record of non-closure, discoverable by every auditor who asks. And the operational risk is unchanged by any of it: the misconfiguration remains exploitable regardless of how well it is reported.

**Currency caveat on this section.** Enforcement mechanics are stated at the level of the governing statute and standing OMB policy as of this document's date. Directive status, deadlines, and reporting regimes change; confirm current CISA directive status and OMB memoranda before this section becomes the basis of a compliance strategy or a remediation-funding argument.
